sections.heading: Learning, work and the European journey
paragraphs: The opening gives Cromwell’s ambition a practical setting. The hammering in his father’s smithy interrupts his reading, and the workmen answer his complaints with jokes about what learning is worth. The opposition is between two activities within the same household: the trade that supports him and the books through which he hopes to change his position. Hodge supplies a comic view of the young scholar’s aspirations.

The subsequent movement between England and continental Europe brings the play into the world of merchants, travellers, bills and personal introductions. Advancement depends on acquiring useful knowledge and on finding people willing to offer employment, credit or protection. These early episodes matter later, when the successful Cromwell has the means to repay obligations incurred before he possessed office or influence.

sections.heading: Merchants, creditors and the Banister plot
paragraphs: The secondary story of Banister gives debt two sharply different human agents. Bagot uses the ruined merchant’s liabilities as an opportunity for profit, whereas Friskiball responds to hardship with assistance. Their actions supply concrete instances of the difference between having a legal claim on another person and choosing how to exercise it. The movement of the Banister family between London and Antwerp connects this subplot to Cromwell’s travels.

Friskiball’s later reversal of fortune allows the same relationship to be tested from the opposite direction. Cromwell can then demonstrate whether prosperity has altered his memory of assistance received. Following these encounters in sequence makes the recurring gifts and repayments easier to understand than treating them as incidental interruptions to the political biography.

sections.heading: History and the play
paragraphs: The historical Thomas Cromwell served Henry VIII as a royal minister and played a central part in the religious and administrative changes of the 1530s. His execution took place on Tower Hill on 28 July 1540. The play organises that career around selected personal encounters and a conspiracy, giving a much simpler explanation of his fall than the political record supports.

In the final movement, statements attributed to Cromwell become evidence against him, while expressions of generosity to his servants are interpreted as signs of a guilty conscience. The audience has already seen conduct that can be read differently. So the handling of testimony is central to the ending: we watch the case against Buckingham being put together.

sections.heading: The Petition of Right and constitutional disagreement
paragraphs: The Petition of Right arose from disputes over taxation, imprisonment and the use of royal power. Presented in 1628, it challenged taxation without parliamentary consent, arbitrary imprisonment, the billeting of soldiers and the imposition of martial law in peacetime. Charles’s responses therefore belong to a specific negotiation about the rights of subjects and the government’s need for money; they are not simply general declarations about monarchy.

The two answers included in this selection allow the form of a royal response to be examined as well as its argument. Official wording had consequences because king and Parliament were disputing what counted as a binding concession. Reading these documents in order helps explain why apparent agreement did not remove the differences that continued into the following decade.

sections.heading: Private correspondence made public
paragraphs: Letters and instructions need a different kind of reading from proclamations and parliamentary answers. A message to Henrietta Maria presumes knowledge shared by husband and wife; an official declaration addresses a wider audience and is designed for circulation. Neither form provides unmediated access to the writer’s thoughts. Recipient, purpose and the circumstances of preservation affect what can reasonably be concluded from it.

The royal papers captured after the Battle of Naseby in June 1645 made this distinction politically urgent. Correspondence intended for restricted use passed into enemy hands and was published by Parliament. The resulting public evidence was also selected and presented as an argument against the king. The edition’s attention to provenance is especially useful when a private document has reached the reader through an adversary’s publication.

sections.heading: Trial, execution and the royal image
paragraphs: At his trial in Westminster Hall in January 1649, Charles challenged the court’s authority and refused to enter a plea. The exchanges consequently concern jurisdiction as well as the accusations against him. The death warrant records the decision to execute him and the commissioners who authorised it; it should be distinguished from the king’s own reported words on the scaffold on 30 January.

Eikon Basilike belongs to the struggle over how that death would be remembered. Published in 1649 as a presentation of the king’s private meditations and sufferings, it became associated with the image of Charles as a Christian martyr. John Gauden’s claim to authorship makes attribution a substantial historical problem. The selection prints it separately, so this famous royal voice is kept apart from documents Charles certainly wrote or spoke.

sections.heading: An unprinted play
paragraphs: The principal witness is British Library Harley MS 7368, a theatrical manuscript containing the original draft, revisions and interventions by several writers. Its physical arrangement supplies evidence that a later printed edition could not preserve in the same way: passages have been cancelled, replacements inserted and wording altered. A continuous modern reading text is therefore an editorial arrangement of a document that records more than one stage of work.

The letters used to distinguish the hands are scholarly identifiers. Hand S is associated with Anthony Munday; Hand C is an unidentified theatrical scribe whose corrections include changes to the contribution called Hand D. The identification of a person with a hand and the decision about how to print that person’s contribution are related questions, but they are not identical.

sections.heading: The strangers’ scene
paragraphs: The crowd’s grievance is expressed through complaints about food, employment and the presence of foreign residents. More first asks the insurgents to recognise their own difficulty in controlling the people they have assembled. He then explains that violence against one group establishes a precedent that can be turned against others. The speech connects the immediate disturbance to the breakdown of the authority on which the citizens themselves depend.

Its appeal to imagine exile comes within that argument. More asks where the rioters would go if they were banished and what treatment they would expect on arriving abroad. The scene ends by returning from imagined displacement to the practical steps of submission, mediation and a request for mercy. Reading the whole exchange preserves both its defence of vulnerable strangers and its insistence on civic obedience.

sections.heading: Censorship, attribution and performance evidence
paragraphs: Edmund Tilney, the Master of the Revels, objected to the insurrection material and ordered substantial alteration. His intervention is surviving evidence of theatrical censorship in practice. It does not, by itself, supply a complete account of what happened afterwards. No early performance is recorded, and the manuscript’s revisions cannot establish that a particular reconstructed version was actually staged.

Hand D is widely attributed to Shakespeare, but the attribution should remain visible as an attribution. The argument combines handwriting, spelling and literary evidence; the small number of securely surviving Shakespeare signatures limits direct comparison. The three pages are consequently important both as a possible autograph contribution and as part of a larger collaborative play whose other writers, scenes and revisions must also be considered.

sections.heading: The Children of Paul’s and the first printing
paragraphs: George Eld printed the play in 1607 under the longer title The Puritan; or, the Widow of Watling Street. Its title page names the Children of Paul’s as the performing company. This matters because it puts the play with a company of boy actors, and not with Shakespeare’s own company. The initials W. S. cannot be assessed in isolation from that information.

The play’s later publication history explains why it continued to be encountered as Shakespeare. It appeared in the enlarged Third Folio in 1664 and in subsequent collections before being treated among the disputed works. The modern attribution to Middleton rests on the play’s style and its likeness to his other work; the initials settle nothing.

sections.heading: The widow’s household and competing marriages
paragraphs: The opening mourning scene immediately divides the household. Lady Plus makes emphatic declarations of grief, Sir Godfrey supplies examples of other widows, and the children respond in ways that expose their different expectations of life after the father’s death. Moll’s interest in marriage is particularly practical: her negotiations with Sir John Pennydub include a coach, servants, clothes and money of her own to spend.

Courtship therefore involves a series of proposed settlements, not a single romantic pursuit. The established suitors offer one set of possibilities; Pyeboard’s associates manufacture another. Changes of intention are followed closely enough for the audience to compare what the characters initially profess with the material advantages and predictions that subsequently persuade them.

sections.heading: Pyeboard’s tricks
paragraphs: The supposed supernatural evidence depends on actions the audience can follow. A chain is stolen before its recovery is presented as a demonstration of unusual knowledge. The conspirators prepare what their victims will see and then supply an explanation that makes the prepared event appear miraculous. Their success relies on control of information and timing, as much as on the victims’ readiness to believe.

Pyeboard’s skill also extends to ordinary social emergencies, including escape from officers seeking payment of debt. His inventive language can change a listener’s understanding of who he is and why he is present. The comedy repeatedly places this resourcefulness beside his precarious circumstances. Reading his financial difficulties alongside the conjuring plot gives a fuller account of his conduct than describing him only as a clever trickster.

sections.heading: The title page’s claim of revision
paragraphs: Thomas Creede’s 1595 title page presents W. S. as the person who oversaw and corrected the play. That wording leaves a distinction between original composition and later preparation for publication. It does not straightforwardly identify W. S. as the sole dramatist. Proposals involving Shakespeare, another writer with the same initials, or an earlier author must account for the limited claim the surviving book actually makes.

A manuscript note by George Buc on one surviving copy has prompted discussion of Charles Tilney, while shared passages and stylistic similarities have led scholars towards Greene and Peele. These are different kinds of evidence. Its inclusion in the enlarged Third Folio of 1664 shows what a later publisher decided; it says nothing about who wrote it.

sections.heading: Geography within the British origin story
paragraphs: The division among Brutus’s sons connects family inheritance with a legendary account of the island’s territories. Locrine, Camber and Albanact do not inhabit an accurately reconstructed early Britain: their story belongs to the inherited tradition of Trojan ancestry and named founders. Classical gods, foreign invaders and British place names coexist within that dramatic world.

The ending similarly attaches a personal death to geography. Sabren, the child of Locrine and Estrild, gives her name to the river associated with her drowning. This is an explanatory legend about a place, not evidence for an actual ancient dynasty. Keeping that distinction in view makes it easier to follow why the tragedy moves from the division of a kingdom to the naming of a river.

sections.heading: Dumb shows and comic scenes
paragraphs: Before the action of each act, Ate introduces a short emblematic performance and explains its relevance. These dumb shows give the audience advance information about patterns of aggression, betrayal or reversal. Their classical examples establish comparisons through visible actions, adding a second level of presentation to the speeches and battles in the main plot.

Strumbo’s scenes offer a different register. His trade, appetite, courtship and fear of death produce practical concerns that sit beside the rulers’ elaborate speeches. When he avoids destruction by pretending to be dead, survival takes precedence over military reputation. The alternation between this comic material and the formal lamentation of the royal characters is part of the play’s structure and should not disappear from an account concerned only with its legendary sources.

sections.heading: Authorship
paragraphs: The 1605 quarto was printed by Thomas Creede for Nathaniel Butter. It names William Shakespeare in full and states that the play was performed by the King’s Men. Butter later published the 1608 quarto of King Lear, making him a bookseller with a documented connection to Shakespeare’s printed work. The attribution is therefore a real feature of an early edition, even though it has not secured the play a generally accepted place in the canon.

The London Prodigal was omitted from the 1623 First Folio, then included among the additions to the Third Folio in 1664. The company attribution has attracted much less dispute than the author’s name. A play could belong to Shakespeare’s company without being written by him, and its absence from the Folio is evidence to weigh, not a final answer.

sections.heading: Credit
paragraphs: Flowerdale’s supposed prosperity is repeatedly established through reports of assets, trade and inheritance. Other people must decide whether to trust those reports and whether to risk their own money or reputation on his behalf. Marriage negotiations become part of this economy because a prospective husband’s financial standing is material evidence about the future he can offer a household.

The appearance of officers at the wedding brings those claims into direct conflict with enforceable debts. A ceremony intended to confirm a new social position instead exposes the liabilities behind it. Following who lends, guarantees, passes on or withholds money makes the action clear: in this play debts have consequences on stage.

sections.heading: The father’s disguise
paragraphs: Flowerdale’s father watches events under another identity, creating a difference between what the young man believes about his family and what the audience knows. His presence allows conduct to be observed when an expected source of authority and rescue appears to have been removed. The device also postpones recognition and makes the eventual restoration of a family relationship a staged event.

Luce’s disguise has another purpose. It enables her to remain near a husband who has rejected her and to intervene without being recognised as his wife. The two disguises should consequently be followed separately: one involves concealed paternal judgement, the other continued practical assistance. Together they make the ending depend on the disclosure of identities as well as on Flowerdale’s declaration that he will change.

sections.heading: Land and status
paragraphs: The first exchange introduces property before it turns fully to adultery. Franklin brings Arden news of a royal grant of former abbey lands, but Arden is preoccupied with Alice and Mosbie. This juxtaposition matters because the play supplies grievances against Arden beyond his wife’s desire to be rid of him. His position as a landowner places him in relationships with people whose material interests differ from his own.

Greene joins the conspiracy because of a dispute over land, while the sailor Reede confronts Arden about the loss of his holding and its consequences for his family. These encounters do not excuse the murder. They do give the central household a specific economic setting and explain why the conspiracy can recruit people who have no personal investment in Alice’s affair.

sections.heading: The conspirators’ motives
paragraphs: The participants do not all want the same result from Arden’s death. Alice wants freedom to marry Mosbie; the hired killers seek payment; Michael is encouraged through the prospect of marrying Susan, Mosbie’s sister. Promises of money, affection and advancement keep the plot moving, but they also make its members dependent on one another’s reliability. An agreement made in one scene can become a source of anxiety in the next.

Black Will and Shakebag repeatedly encounter practical obstacles to the work for which they have been hired. Travel, weather, bystanders and Arden’s changing movements interfere with their plans. These delays give the audience information the intended victim does not possess and create repeated occasions on which the conspirators must improvise. The eventual killing inside the house follows a long sequence of failed attempts in less controllable settings.

sections.heading: The household and the evidence
paragraphs: Once Arden is dead, the conspirators have to manage physical traces as well as their accounts of what happened. The moved body, the blood in the house and the footprints in the snow are how the murder is found out. Alice’s attempts to explain Arden’s absence must compete with what other characters have seen and with what the search reveals.

The closing account of punishments places the staged murder within a larger record of discovery and retribution. It is useful to distinguish this reported conclusion from the action the audience has witnessed. The play dramatises private conversations and competing motives that a chronicle could not independently certify, even while presenting itself as a tragedy based on a known local crime.

sections.heading: Four volumes from a five-book publishing sequence
paragraphs: The four works collected here first appeared as separate short books: A Christmas Carol in 1843, The Chimes in 1844, The Cricket on the Hearth in 1845, and The Haunted Man and the Ghost’s Bargain in 1848. The intervening Christmas book, The Battle of Life, appeared in 1846 and is not part of this volume. So the collection has four of the five Christmas books.

The books’ original seasonal publication does not mean that all their actions take place on Christmas Day. The Chimes concerns the passage from one year to the next, and The Cricket on the Hearth describes domestic events through the terms of a fairy tale. Reading them together shows the range of stories Dickens published for the Christmas market during these years.

sections.heading: Staves, quarters, chirps and chapters
paragraphs: Each work makes its divisions part of its presentation. A Christmas Carol has five staves, using a musical term to sustain the title’s suggestion of a song. The Chimes is divided into four quarters, corresponding to the striking of a clock. The Cricket on the Hearth has three chirps, while the three chapters of The Haunted Man trace the gift bestowed, diffused and reversed.

These short sequences make useful reading sessions, but their effects differ. Scrooge receives successive visits; Trotty Veck is shown consequences extending beyond the immediate present; John Peerybingle has to reconsider what he thinks he has witnessed; and Redlaw discovers that his bargain affects people beyond himself. The supernatural machinery is different in each book: spirits, goblins of the bells, a cricket, a phantom double.

sections.heading: Households, work and the terms of assistance
paragraphs: The characters’ occupations give the stories concrete social settings. Scrooge employs Bob Cratchit; Trotty works as a porter; John Peerybingle is a carrier; Caleb Plummer makes toys; and Redlaw teaches chemistry. Wages, employment, debt and the maintenance of households remain present even when ghosts, goblins or domestic spirits enter the action. The stories do not take place in a festive interval from material concerns.

They also distinguish different kinds of help. Fezziwig’s treatment of his employees, the wealthy speakers’ advice to Trotty, Caleb’s attempts to protect Bertha, and Milly Swidger’s care for others can be compared through what each person actually does. The collected format makes those comparisons possible without reducing four different narratives to a single general message about Christmas generosity.

sections.heading: Two titles within the 1608 quarto
paragraphs: The book’s main title page calls the work A Yorkshire Tragedy, but an internal heading introduces All’s One and describes it as one of four plays in one. That second heading is evidence for a larger entertainment of which the surviving short tragedy may have been a part. It does not identify the missing companion pieces or establish their authorship.

The first edition was printed by Richard Braddock for Thomas Pavier. Its explicit attribution to Shakespeare, combined with its reference to the King’s Men and the Globe, is unusually substantial contemporary print evidence. Modern scholarship nevertheless generally accepts Middleton’s authorship. The discrepancy is worth preserving: an early publisher’s attribution and the conclusions drawn from later study of the text are separate forms of evidence.

sections.heading: The opening conversation
paragraphs: The first scene is a conversation among servants, with news brought from London, jokes about fashions and reports of the young master’s behaviour. Its comparatively comic manner differs from the scenes that follow. The audience hears of extravagant expenditure, debts and abuse before meeting the family at the centre of those reports. The scene makes the household’s condition a matter of knowledge among servants as well as among their employers.

Reports about a brother at university extend the consequences beyond the immediate family. He has stood security for the Husband and is now endangered by debts contracted on his behalf. When the Master of a College arrives, the prospect of lost education and imprisonment supplies another example of obligations the Husband has allowed other people to bear.

sections.heading: The Husband’s words and actions
paragraphs: The Husband describes the killing of his children as a way of preventing the poverty he has brought upon them. The surrounding action exposes the contradiction in that claim. His wife goes for help, other people step in, and the children he says he is protecting are the ones he attacks. Keeping his speeches distinct from the account supplied by the action is essential to reading the tragedy accurately.

After his capture, the return to the house forces him to look at the results of his conduct. The play ends with the movement towards legal custody and does not stage the historical Calverley’s eventual punishment. Its final concentration is on recognition within the damaged household. That ending is one reason to distinguish the dramatic sequence from a complete documentary account of the 1605 case.

sections.heading: The first quarto and the Elizabethan history play
paragraphs: Cuthbert Burby entered the play in the Stationers’ Register on 1 December 1595 and published it in 1596. The register’s description emphasises Edward, the Black Prince and their war with the French king. Burby also issued Shakespeare plays during the 1590s, including Love’s Labour’s Lost and the second quarto of Romeo and Juliet. Edward III belongs to that commercial world of printed drama, although its first title page does not name an author.

The publication date establishes when the play was in print, not an exact date of composition or first performance. Its later exclusion from the First Folio and the modern arguments for shared authorship are further stages in the text’s history. They should be distinguished from the historical fourteenth-century events represented on stage.

sections.heading: A king commissions a love poem
paragraphs: In the Countess episode, Edward employs Lodowick to put his desire into verse. Their exchange brings the making of poetry directly onto the stage: the king demands praise adequate to the woman he wants, finds conventional descriptions insufficient, and attempts to direct another person’s words. Literary composition becomes one of the services royal power expects to command.

The Countess’s resistance makes the limits of that expectation explicit. She is already married, as Edward is, and her replies force him to acknowledge obligations his pursuit attempts to disregard. The episode is therefore not a detachable account of a royal courtship. It shows the king issuing instructions and encountering an answer that he cannot honourably compel his subject to change.

sections.heading: Battle, surrender and the treatment of civilians
paragraphs: The campaign scenes use messengers, challenges, reports and changes of location to represent warfare across a large area. The Black Prince’s experience is central, but the action also includes French rulers, soldiers and inhabitants of besieged Calais. Keeping track of who is speaking and where a report originates helps separate an announced expectation from an event actually shown to have occurred.

Calais introduces questions that victory alone cannot settle. The play shows poor inhabitants expelled from the town because they cannot contribute to its defence and must still be fed. Later, the six citizens who offer themselves to save the town face Edward’s anger, while Philippa argues for mercy. These scenes place the use of power over surrendered or defenceless people beside the account of military achievement.

sections.heading: Short rhymes and longer formal structures
paragraphs: The term Skeltonic is useful for the short lines and extended runs of rhyme found in much of Skelton’s best-known verse, but it does not describe everything he wrote. The Bowge of Court uses seven-line rhyme-royal stanzas, and the elegies require attention to their formal organisation as well as their historical occasions. Changes of line length and stanza form are part of the range represented by the selection.

Colin Clout explicitly anticipates an objection to the roughness of its verse and answers that an irregular surface can carry substantial matter. Its sequences of rhyme work alongside changes of speaker, reported complaint and abrupt questions. Following the sentence across the short lines is particularly useful: a line ending supplies emphasis without necessarily marking the end of a thought.

sections.heading: A dream of the court and a gathering at an alehouse
paragraphs: The Bowge of Court presents courtly dependence through a dream of a ship and the people encountered aboard it. Personified qualities appear as named figures, and the speaker has to work out what each of them wants. The account of the dream is also an account of uncertainty: apparent friendship, promises of favour and information about rivals cannot simply be taken at their stated value.

The Tunning of Elinour Rumming moves to another setting, concentrating on an ale seller and the women who come to drink. Clothes, bodily appearance, household goods and items offered in payment accumulate in its descriptions. The contrast with the court poem makes it possible to compare the poet’s treatment of social display across very different surroundings, while retaining the distinct form and purpose of each work.

sections.heading: Religious language, mourning and satire
paragraphs: Philip Sparrow begins from grief for a pet bird and uses words and forms associated with religious observance. Its English verse incorporates Latin phrases, names of birds and an extensive display of remembered reading. The shifts in scale, from the small dead creature to the elaborate verbal response, are features of the poem itself; they should not be mistaken for a simple anecdote about its author’s life.

The political and religious satires likewise move between learned expression and reported everyday speech. A complaint voiced within a poem is not automatically Skelton speaking without mediation. Attention to quotation, questions and changes of address helps distinguish the speaker’s position from the claims he reports. The edition’s headnotes and declared extract boundaries provide the setting needed to read these different forms together without treating every piece as complete.

sections.heading: Sleepy Hollow
paragraphs: The Legend of Sleepy Hollow appeared in 1820 as part of Washington Irving’s Sketch Book. Its rural New York community has a remembered Dutch past, local stories about the Revolutionary War and a schoolmaster from Connecticut who listens readily to supernatural accounts. The Headless Horseman is introduced through the community’s storytelling before Ichabod Crane encounters what he believes to be the apparition.

The autumn gathering at the Van Tassels’ supplies food, music, dancing and further stories before Ichabod’s journey home. Those details make the tale especially appropriate to an autumn collection, but Irving does not identify the occasion as a Halloween party. The narrative also preserves competing explanations for Ichabod’s disappearance. Its final reports and the teller’s postscript matter when distinguishing the written story from adaptations that settle the mystery differently.

sections.heading: Kinds of story
paragraphs: The collection’s haunted houses, apparitions and violent confessions do not all operate in the same way. Poe’s The Tell-Tale Heart and The Black Cat give their accounts through narrators implicated in the violence they describe. The Fall of the House of Usher instead brings an observer into another household. Comparing who tells the story, what that person has seen and what they attempt to explain is a useful route through the three selections.

Gilman’s The Yellow Wall-Paper, first published in 1892, records a woman’s experience of confinement and treatment through writing she conceals from those around her. Lovecraft’s The Outsider, published in Weird Tales in April 1926, follows an isolated narrator whose understanding of his situation changes through an encounter with other people. Their inclusion extends the collection beyond conventional tales of a ghost returning to a familiar home.

sections.heading: The stories and the holiday’s history
paragraphs: American Halloween took its present form gradually; it is not one tradition handed down unchanged. Seasonal parties, games, disguises, commercial decorations and organised trick-or-treating have different histories. Evidence from a nineteenth-century story therefore cannot establish that the full modern set of customs was already in place when it was written.

The anthology’s publication histories and chronology support two related sequences: the development of the short fiction and the later uses of that fiction in seasonal reading. A reader can follow the stories in their original contexts, compare particular devices across writers, or choose a group for an October reading session. The twelve complete texts remain the centre of the collection, with the historical material explaining the later seasonal connections.
